newsitem.title: USA: Alternate jurors seated in Simpson case, trial next.
newsitem.headline: Alternate jurors seated in Simpson case, trial next.

text.p: Jury selection ended in the O.J. Simpson civil case on Monday with the swearing-in of eight alternates -- five of them white -- to back up the mostly white, 12-person panel already seated.

The end of the month-long process cleared the way for opening statements to begin on Wednesday in the wrongful death lawsuit against Simpson for the death of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman.

Meanwhile, Simpson, in a TV interview to be aired this week, said he expected to win his civil trial and predicted "retribution" for those who tried to convict him in the criminal case. He did not elaborate.

Simpson, a former football star, actor and television pitchman, was acquitted in October 1995 of the stabbing murders. If found responsible in civil court for the murders, Simpson could be forced to pay millions of dollars in damages to the families of the victims.

Simpson was in court on Monday as Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki empaneled the five men and three women who will serve as alternate jurors. In addition to the five whites, there was also one black, one Hispanic and one Asian.

The alternates will replace any of the original 12 jurors who drop out for any reason, such as sickness or misconduct. That panel consists of eight whites, one black, one Hispanic, one person who is part white and part Hispanic and one Asian-black.

The racial makeup of the jury could be crucial, since during questioning, potential jurors were divided largely along racial lines, with blacks tending to believe Simpson was innocent and most whites believing he probably was guilty. Simpson is black; the victims were white.

Fujisaki's courtroom will be dark on Tuesday to allow attorneys to prepare their opening statements and set up video equipment. The statements were scheduled for Wednesday, after the judge rules on several motions filed by the plaintiffs, including one to bar defence lawyers from referring to a former detective's no contest plea to perjury.

Mark Fuhrman, one of the first detectives at the murder scene on June 12, 1994, and the man who discovered some of the key evidence that night, entered his plea this month and was sentenced to three years probation and fined $200.

He was accused by lawyers in the criminal case of being a racist, rogue cop who planted the now-famous bloody glove found on Simpson's estate. After the defence produced audiotapes of him using racial epithets, he asserted his Fifth Amendment rights against self-incrimination.
Since then, he has retired from the police department and moved to Idaho. In a recent televised interview, he denied planting evidence and apologised for using racial slurs.

Simpson's lawyer, Robert Baker, argued on Monday that Fuhrman "will be a witness in this case regardless of whether he is present or not present" in the courtroom and thus the defence should be allowed to refer to both his perjury plea and his alleged racist views.

In Simpson's televised interview, "O.J. in Black and White," part of a special to be shown on Wednesday night on the CBS News Extra programme, he told correspondent Bill Whitaker that "the best part about this civil case is in many ways I think I'll be vindicated and there'll be retribution."
Asked against whom there would be retribution, he said: "Members of the prosecution team and the L.A.P.D. Members, not the whole offices."
